companyDossiers.name: NeuroPace
companyDossiers.summary: NeuroPace’s progress centers on detecting patient-specific activity, delivering stimulation and sustaining long-term therapy, rather than increasing a probe-count maximum.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Inventor Robert Fischell founded the company. Brian Litt contributed licensed technology; Emory records one historical license that is no longer active.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: Incorporation in 1997 preceded the original RNS approval in 2013. The published record then expands through device iteration and long-term clinical follow-up.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Implanted sensing and programmable detection trigger responsive stimulation; patient uploads let clinicians review selected electrographic recordings and adjust settings.

timeline.title: Company incorporated
timeline.text: The date is recorded in the filed corporate certificate.

timeline.title: Original RNS approval
timeline.text: FDA approved adjunctive therapy for a defined adult focal-epilepsy population.

timeline.title: Memory and battery iteration
timeline.text: Next generation doubled memory and increased estimated longevity at medium settings.

timeline.title: Nine-year follow-up published
timeline.text: Prospective open-label follow-up examines long-term outcomes.

changes.title: Scale useful time, not contacts
changes.text: The 2018 generation emphasized longer replacement intervals and more stored brain data in the same package.

changes.title: Separate detection from prediction
changes.text: RNS reacts to configured abnormal patterns; avoid describing it as a universally reliable predictor that prevents every seizure.

gaps: Emory’s license is historical and explicitly no longer active.
No single academic laboratory is established as the sole source of the complete RNS system.
The 8.4-year figure was a settings-dependent battery estimate.

companyDossiers.name: NeuroOne Medical Technologies
companyDossiers.summary: NeuroOne links an explicitly licensed university thin-film technology to clinical development and a workflow in which one implanted electrode can both localize and treat tissue.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Williams and Garell translated operating-room observations into thinner, more conformable electrodes. UW links this work to NeuroOne’s early launch.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: WARF licensed specified patents; Mayo separately licensed know-how and supported development. These are documented agreements, not inferred affiliation links.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Cortical sensing progressed into a product family including OneRF. Its sEEG probe first supports diagnostic localization and then RF lesioning with temperature monitoring.

timeline.title: Clinical need becomes thin-film development
timeline.text: UW dates Williams’ arrival to 2003 and the resulting company launch to 2009.

timeline.title: Two distinct academic agreements
timeline.text: WARF patent license on October 1; Mayo license/development agreement effective October 3.

timeline.title: Mayo agreement restated
timeline.text: Filed agreement preserves the 2014 effective date and defines subsequent development rights.

timeline.title: Cortical electrode clearance
timeline.text: FDA records K192764 clearance.

timeline.title: OneRF clearance
timeline.text: FDA clears the lesioning system using an implanted sEEG-RF probe.

changes.title: Expand function at the same implant
changes.text: The clinical workflow can move from recording/localization to RF treatment through the implanted probe.

changes.title: Make the license boundary visible
changes.text: WARF’s patent grant is US-limited; Mayo know-how and development are a separate agreement.

gaps: The university’s 2009 launch is not necessarily the incorporation date of today’s public legal entity.
Ablation is an intended irreversible therapeutic action, distinct from recording or chronic closed-loop stimulation.
Patent licensing does not imply every current product embodies every original patent.

companyDossiers.name: Ripple Neuro
companyDossiers.summary: Ripple combines neural-engineering expertise with compact acquisition, bidirectional stimulation and investigational implant work. Research products and a complete approved human therapy remain different categories.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Hiatt trained under Normann at Utah; Wilder’s Utah doctoral work concerned neuro-assistive software before his 2009 Ripple start.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: Government accounts emphasize SBIR/STTR-supported development. The 2015 HAPTIX effort paired muscle recording with peripheral nerve stimulation.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Link R-32 uses inductive power and transcutaneous data with custom leads. Its specified bandwidth is suited to EMG/LFP-scale signals rather than high-rate extracellular spikes.

timeline.title: Founding accounts differ
timeline.text: Official LinkedIn says 2004; the government award story says 2005.

timeline.title: Software expertise joins
timeline.text: Wilder joined to develop neural visualization and stimulation software.

timeline.title: HAPTIX implant program
timeline.text: Company describes MIRA myoelectric recording and SARA nerve-stimulation development.

timeline.title: SBIR/STTR translation recognized
timeline.text: Government account documents research-product and implant-development commercialization.

changes.title: Move electronics closer to signals
changes.text: Digital front ends and compact processing reduce the burden of large laboratory equipment.

changes.title: Wireless power changes the implant tradeoff
changes.text: The R-32 avoids an implanted battery and uses an external magnetically coupled transceiver; coupling and bandwidth remain system constraints.

gaps: Exact founding year remains unresolved between two primary accounts.
The inspected sources establish staff training, not an exclusive University of Utah spinout/license.
The dated MIRA/SARA specifications were development claims.
Ripple Neuro’s research products should not be conflated with every project of related Ripple companies.

companyDossiers.name: Amber Therapeutics
companyDossiers.summary: Amber reuses an adaptive implant research platform originally developed around brain stimulation, then changes the anatomical target, therapy logic and commercial organization.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Oxford and Bioinduction extended Picostim into the configurable DyNeuMo platform. Denison brought industry device-engineering experience to the academic collaboration.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: The 2021 Oxford spinout brought engineering, urology and surgery founders together. Acquiring Bioinduction in 2023 internalized platform and manufacturing capabilities.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Amber-UI applies the platform to two pudendal-nerve leads, using sensors and configurable therapy algorithms to investigate urinary control.

timeline.title: Oxford spinout founded
timeline.text: Founders are Crawley, Denison, De Wachter and Knowles.

timeline.title: Brain research platform reported
timeline.text: Oxford describes the Picostim-DyNeuMo first-human research implantation for MSA.

timeline.title: AURA-2 begins
timeline.text: The platform is used for a peripheral urinary-incontinence feasibility study.

timeline.title: Bioinduction acquisition announced
timeline.text: Amber combines therapy development with the platform supplier.

timeline.title: Preliminary AURA-2 findings
timeline.text: University account reports early feasibility and adaptive-algorithm testing.

changes.title: Reuse a platform, change the therapy
changes.text: Shared electronics and software configurability permit a shift from cranial research to pudendal-nerve therapy; clinical evidence must be generated for the new use.

changes.title: Acquire development and manufacturing
changes.text: The Bioinduction transaction adds people, quality systems and production capabilities to the therapy company.

gaps: The spinout source does not disclose specific university patent-license terms.
Denison’s prior Medtronic role is not evidence of Medtronic-to-Amber IP transfer.
Early AURA-2 results do not establish broad clinical effectiveness or market approval.

companyDossiers.name: Saluda Medical
companyDossiers.summary: Saluda’s defining advance is measuring the spinal response to each stimulus and using it for feedback. This provides a clear example of progress that electrode counts alone miss.

stages.title: Research roots
stages.text: Parker and colleagues reported human spinal ECAP measurements online in 2011, with the paper appearing in 2012. This supplied a measurable response to stimulation.

stages.title: Translation
stages.text: The NICTA spinout was announced in February2013. The Australian patent office subsequently recorded assignments of specific applications from NICTA to Saluda.

stages.title: Interface built
stages.text: Evoke’s implanted controller compares the measured activation after a pulse with a clinician-selected target and adjusts stimulation current.

timeline.title: Human spinal ECAP paper
timeline.text: Online and print dates refer to the same primary study.

timeline.title: NICTA spinout
timeline.text: A contemporary government speech records the spinout announcement.

timeline.title: Patent assignments published
timeline.text: The patent office records selected NICTA applications assigned to Saluda.

timeline.title: Founder moves to scientific role
timeline.text: Parker transitions from CEO to chief scientific officer as the company advances toward commercialization.

timeline.title: Evoke FDA approval
timeline.text: Original PMA authorizes the system for specified chronic intractable trunk/limb pain.

timeline.title: Limited US release begins
timeline.text: Company announces initial US commercialization.

changes.title: Control a measured neural response
changes.text: The loop regulates evoked activation rather than leaving stimulus current fixed while body position and coupling vary.

changes.title: Separate biomarker from clinical outcome
changes.text: ECAP measures recruited neural response. Pain relief remains a patient outcome requiring its own clinical evidence.

gaps: Data61 is a retrospective organizational label; NICTA is the historically correct 2013 name.
The patent office records individual assignments; a complete transfer contract and current claim-to-product mapping were not assessed.
ECAPs are compound responses, not single-neuron recordings or a direct pain meter.
